title: Microsoft to Switch On Anthropic's Claude by Default for UK Copilot Tenants on Dec. 9
summary: Microsoft switches on Anthropic Claude by default for UK Copilot tenants
detailed: Microsoft will begin routing UK organizations' Microsoft 365 Copilot traffic through Anthropic's Claude models by default on December 9, converting administrative inaction into consent for a large installed base of business and public-sector accounts.

On its documentation page for Claude in Microsoft online services, the company states that Anthropic models used in Copilot, Researcher, Copilot Studio and the Power Platform are "currently excluded from the EU Data Boundary," the framework under which Microsoft pledges to keep customer data processed inside the bloc.

At the same time it is retiring the narrower option that allowed Claude only within Copilot inside the Microsoft 365 applications, so tenants without a selection of their own will move to all users rather than a restricted pool.
The control sits in the Microsoft 365 admin center under Copilot, then Settings, then AI providers operating as Microsoft subprocessors.
sentences: Microsoft will begin routing UK organizations' Microsoft 365 Copilot traffic through Anthropic's Claude models by default on December 9, converting administrative inaction into consent for a large installed base of business and public-sector accounts.
The change, detailed in message center post MC1546435, affects every UK tenant whose administrators have not yet made a selection in the AI providers settings.
Tenants that leave the field untouched will be moved to all users on the effective date.
Organizations in the European Union are unaffected: Claude remains switched off there until an administrator explicitly enables it.
Microsoft attributes the regional split to its data-residency commitments.

On its documentation page for Claude in Microsoft online services, the company states that Anthropic models used in Copilot, Researcher, Copilot Studio and the Power Platform are "currently excluded from the EU Data Boundary," the framework under which Microsoft pledges to keep customer data processed inside the bloc.
The setting therefore defaults to "No users" for customers in the EU, the European Free Trade Association states and the UK.
In other commercial regions Claude is already enabled by default, and data is processed in the United States.
Because Britain sits outside the EU Data Boundary, Microsoft is withdrawing the UK exception.

At the same time it is retiring the narrower option that allowed Claude only within Copilot inside the Microsoft 365 applications, so tenants without a selection of their own will move to all users rather than a restricted pool.
UK administrators who want Claude kept off, or limited to particular people, must choose "No users" or specify individual users and groups before December 9.
The control sits in the Microsoft 365 admin center under Copilot, then Settings, then AI providers operating as Microsoft subprocessors.
Only AI administrators and global administrators can change it.
EU organizations that previously opted in under Anthropic's separate commercial terms will have to opt in again, according to the company.
Note: Based on Microsoft message center post MC1546435 and the company's Claude documentation page.
A separate track governs Anthropic models that carry data-retention requirements, such as Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5.

Those are covered by Anthropic's own terms rather than Microsoft's data protection commitments, with most inputs and outputs retained for up to 30 days, and administrators must still switch them on themselves.
Neither the message center post nor the documentation addresses Microsoft 365 Personal or Family, since both cover managed work accounts only.
The shift matters beyond a single toggle.

Copilot is Microsoft's principal vehicle for selling generative AI into corporate productivity suites, and the underlying model has become a competitive battleground as Microsoft balances its longstanding OpenAI partnership against a multi-vendor strategy.
For UK enterprises, particularly those in regulated sectors that vet where data is processed, the default now cuts the other way: silence produces activation rather than exclusion.

Compliance, legal and procurement teams that assumed a do-nothing posture was the cautious one will need to revisit their Copilot governance before the December date, and multinationals running a single tenant configuration across Britain and the EU will find the two jurisdictions pointing in opposite directions.
